claim: S100A9 potently amplifies inflammation via Toll-like receptor four.
source: S100A9 is one such multifunctional protein. It potently amplifies inflammation via Toll-like receptor four and is antimicrobial as part of a heterocomplex with S100A8.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of S100A9.

claim: S100A9 is antimicrobial as part of a heterocomplex with S100A8.
source: It potently amplifies inflammation via Toll-like receptor four and is antimicrobial as part of a heterocomplex with S100A8.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of the S100A8/A9 complex.

claim: S100A9 is readily degraded by proteolysis.
source: These two functions are seemingly regulated by proteolysis: S100A9 is readily degraded, while S100A8/S100A9 is resistant.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of S100A9.

claim: S100A8/S100A9 is resistant to proteolytic degradation.
source: These two functions are seemingly regulated by proteolysis: S100A9 is readily degraded, while S100A8/S100A9 is resistant.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of the S100A8/A9 complex.

claim: S100A9 evolved both proinflammatory and antimicrobial functions from a weakly proinflammatory, proteolytically resistant amniote ancestor.
source: We take an evolutionary biochemical approach to show that S100A9 evolved both functions and lost proteolytic resistance from a weakly proinflammatory, proteolytically resistant amniote ancestor.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ancestral sequence reconstruction and functional assays.

claim: S100A9 lost proteolytic resistance from a proteolytically resistant amniote ancestor.
source: We take an evolutionary biochemical approach to show that S100A9 evolved both functions and lost proteolytic resistance from a weakly proinflammatory, proteolytically resistant amniote ancestor.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on ancestral sequence reconstruction and proteolytic resistance assays.

claim: A historical substitution at position 63 has pleiotropic effects on S100A9 proinflammatory activity and proteolytic resistance.
source: We identify a historical substitution that has pleiotropic effects on S100A9 proinflammatory activity and proteolytic resistance but has little effect on S100A8/S100A9 antimicrobial activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on mutagenesis experiments and functional assays.

claim: The substitution at position 63 has little effect on S100A8/S100A9 antimicrobial activity.
source: We identify a historical substitution that has pleiotropic effects on S100A9 proinflammatory activity and proteolytic resistance but has little effect on S100A8/S100A9 antimicrobial activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on antimicrobial assays of mutant proteins.

claim: Mammals evolved S100A8/S100A9 antimicrobial and S100A9 proinflammatory activities concomitantly with a proteolytic 'timer' to selectively regulate S100A9.
source: We thus propose that mammals evolved S100A8/S100A9 antimicrobial and S100A9 proinflammatory activities concomitantly with a proteolytic 'timer' to selectively regulate S100A9.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the evolutionary and functional data presented in the study.

claim: The same mutation can have pleiotropic effects on one functional state of a protein but not another, facilitating the evolution of multifunctionality.
source: This highlights how the same mutation can have pleiotropic effects on one functional state of a protein but not another, thus facilitating the evolution of multifunctionality.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the specific findings about the M63F mutation.

claim: As a homodimer, A9 potently activates inflammation via Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4).
source: As a homodimer, A9 potently activates inflammation via Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) (Vogl et al., 2012; Källberg et al., 2012; Duan et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2006; Schiopu and Cotoi, 2013; Laouedj et al., 2017; He et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Björk et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2015; Stríz and Trebichavský, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: As a heterocomplex with S100A8 (A8/A9), S100A9 is antimicrobial.
source: As a heterocomplex with S100A8 (A8/A9, also known as calprotectin), it is antimicrobial (Figure 1a; Besold et al., 2018a; Hadley et al., 2018; Damo et al., 2013; Clark et al., 2016; Besold et al., 2018b; Nakashige et al., 2016; Hayden et al., 2013; Nakashige et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Brunjes Brophy et al., 2013; Brophy et al., 2012; Baker et al., 2017; Gagnon et al., 2015; Nisapakultorn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: A9 exacerbates endotoxin-induced shock in mice.
source: A9 exacerbates endotoxin-induced shock in mice (Vogl et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both A9 and A8/A9 are primary biomarkers for many human inflammatory diseases.
source: Both A9 and A8/A9 are primary biomarkers for many human inflammatory diseases (Vogl et al., 2014; Hara et al., 2012; Obry et al., 2014; Horvath et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of A9 is associated with various cancers, pulmonary disorders, and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Further, dysregulation of A9 is associated with various cancers, pulmonary disorders, and Alzheimer's disease (Källberg et al., 2012; Vogl et al., 2014; Hara et al., 2012; Obry et al., 2014; Horvath et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2009; Averill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A8/A9 antimicrobial activity is mediated by sequestering transition metals through a hexahistidine site and a His3Asp site.
source: The mechanism of A8/A9 antimicrobial activity is well established: it sequesters a variety of transition metals through both a hexahistidine site and a His3Asp site formed at the A8/A9 heterodimer interface, thereby limiting the concentrations of essential microbial nutrients in the extracellular space (Besold et al., 2018a; Hadley et al., 2018; Damo et al., 2013; Clark et al., 2016; Besold et al., 2018b; Nakashige et al., 2016; Hayden et al., 2013; Nakashige et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Brunjes Brophy et al., 2013; Brophy et al., 2012; Baker et al., 2017; Gagnon et al., 2015; Nisapakultorn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature describing the mechanism.

claim: Other S100 proteins exert weaker antimicrobial activity via the His3Asp site.
source: Other S100 proteins exert weaker antimicrobial activity via the His3Asp site, which has lower metal-binding affinity and binds fewer types of transition metals than the A8/A9 hexahistidine site (Nakashige et al., 2016; Hayden et al., 2013; Nakashige et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Brunjes Brophy et al., 2013; Bozzi and Nolan, 2020; Cunden and Nolan, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A9 acts as a Damage-Associated Molecular Pattern (DAMP), activating NF-κB and other cytokines through TLR4.
source: A9 acts as a Damage-Associated Molecular Pattern (DAMP), activating NF-κB and other cytokines through Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) (Vogl et al., 2012; Källberg et al., 2012; Duan et al., 2018; Shepherd et al., 2006; Schiopu and Cotoi, 2013; Laouedj et al., 2017; He et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Björk et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The interaction interface(s), affinity, and stoichiometry for the A9/TLR4 interaction are not known.
source: The interaction interface(s), affinity, and stoichiometry for the A9/TLR4 interaction are not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A small region of A9 has been suggested to form part of the A9/TLR4 binding surface.
source: A small region of A9 has been suggested to form part of the A9/TLR4 binding surface, (Vogl et al., 2018) but no mutant of A9 has been identified that substantially compromises its activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No mutant of A9 has been identified that substantially compromises its activation of TLR4.
source: A small region of A9 has been suggested to form part of the A9/TLR4 binding surface, (Vogl et al., 2018) but no mutant of A9 has been identified that substantially compromises its activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: Neutrophils release multiple proteases along with A9 at sites of inflammation that regulate the inflammatory response.
source: Neutrophils release multiple proteases along with A9 at sites of inflammation that regulate the inflammatory response (Henry et al., 2016; Stapels et al., 2015; Kessenbrock et al., 2011; Heutinck et al., 2010; Janoff, 1972; Jerke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Proteolytic fragments of A9 are sufficient to activate TLR4.
source: Proteolytic fragments of A9 are sufficient to activate TLR4, (Vogl et al., 2018) and proinflammatory stimuli are thought to stabilize A9 homodimers against proteolytic degradation (Riva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Proinflammatory stimuli are thought to stabilize A9 homodimers against proteolytic degradation.
source: Proteolytic fragments of A9 are sufficient to activate TLR4, (Vogl et al., 2018) and proinflammatory stimuli are thought to stabilize A9 homodimers against proteolytic degradation (Riva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A9 and A8 genes are only found together in therian mammals.
source: Second, A9 and A8 genes are only found together in therian mammals (Figure 1b; Loes et al., 2018); therefore the A8/A9 complex could not have arisen earlier than in the ancestor of therian mammals.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous phylogenetic work and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The residues composing the antimicrobial hexahistidine metal-binding site are fully conserved across therian mammals.
source: Lastly, the residues composing the antimicrobial hexahistidine metal-binding site are fully conserved across therian mammals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing sequence alignment.

claim: Cysteine-free opossum A8/A9 formed a heterotetramer (46.8 ± 0.7 kDa) in the presence of calcium.
source: We confirmed that cysteine-free opossum A8/A9 formed a heterotetramer (46.8 ± 0.7 kDa) in the presence of calcium – like the human and mouse proteins (Streicher et al., 2010) – using size exclusion chromatography coupled with multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC MALS, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on SEC MALS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cysteine-free opossum A8/A9 exhibited dose-dependent antimicrobial activity against S. epidermidis.
source: We observed a dose-dependent decrease in S. epidermidis growth in the presence of low micromolar concentrations of cysteine-free opossum A8/A9 (Figure 1c–d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on antimicrobial assay data shown in Figures 1c-d and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The antimicrobial activity of opossum A8/A9 was weaker than that of human A8/A9.
source: The antimicrobial activity of opossum A8/A9 was weaker than that of human A8/A9: opossum A8/A9 delayed bacterial growth, while human A8/A9 both delayed growth and decreased bacterial carrying capacity (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on comparison of antimicrobial assay data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Wildtype opossum A8/A9 had higher antimicrobial activity than cysteine-free opossum A8/A9.
source: We found that wildtype opossum A8/A9 had higher activity than cysteine-free opossum A8/A9 over the concentration range tested (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on antimicrobial assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cysteines present in mouse and opossum A8/A9 play a role in their antimicrobial activity, unlike in human A8/A9.
source: This suggests that the cysteines present in mouse and opossum A8/A9 play a role in their antimicrobial activity, unlike in human A8/A9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wildtype and cysteine-free variants.

claim: AncA8 and ancA9 had average posterior probabilities of 0.88 and 0.83, respectively.
source: AncA8 and ancA9 had average posterior probabilities of 0.88 and 0.83, with sequence similarities to human A8 and A9 of 66% and 64%, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on ancestral sequence reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: AncA8/A9 exhibited potent antimicrobial activity against S. epidermidis comparable to human A8/A9.
source: We observed a potent reduction in S. epidermidis growth comparable to that of human A8/A9 (Figure 1c–d, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on antimicrobial assay data shown in Figures 1c-d and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: AltancA8/A9 exhibited antimicrobial activity similar to opossum A8/A9: it delayed growth but did not ultimately limit bacterial carrying capacity.
source: AltancA8/A9 exhibited antimicrobial activity against S. epidermidis similar to opossum A8/A9: it delayed growth but did not ultimately limit bacterial carrying capacity.
evidence: This is based on antimicrobial assay data comparing altancA8/A9 to opossum A8/A9.

claim: A subset of the ambiguously reconstructed 27 residues between ancA8/A9 and altancA8/A9 are important for A8/A9 antimicrobial activity.
source: While the hexahistidine site residues are conserved in ancA8/A9 and altancA8/A9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), it appears that a subset of the ambiguously reconstructed 27 residues are important for A8/A9 antimicrobial activity, perhaps affecting the orientation and/or affinity of the hexahistidine metal-binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in antimicrobial activity between ancA8/A9 and altancA8/A9.

claim: Human A9 potently activates human, opossum, and chicken TLR4.
source: Our previous work revealed that human A9 potently activates not only human TLR4 in functional assays, but also opossum and chicken TLR4 (Figure 2a; Loes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Chicken MRP126 is a weak activator of all TLR4s, including chicken TLR4.
source: In contrast, chicken MRP126, the sauropsid ortholog of A9s, was found to be a weak activator of all TLR4s, including chicken TLR4.
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous work.

claim: Both human and opossum A9 activate chicken TLR4 better than chicken MRP126 does.
source: Both human and opossum A9 activate chicken TLR4 better than chicken MRP126 does.
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous work.

claim: AncCG had an average posterior probability of 0.86.
source: The average posterior probability of ancCG was 0.86 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on ancestral sequence reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Human A9 potently activated human TLR4, resulting in high levels of NF-κB production.
source: Consistent with previous results, (Loes et al., 2018) we found that human A9 potently activated human TLR4, resulting in high levels of NF-κB production (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Human A8/A9 and opossum A9 exhibited much weaker activity against human TLR4 than human A9.
source: Human A8/A9 and opossum A9 exhibited much weaker activity against human TLR4.
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data.

claim: AncA9, altancA9, ancCG, and altancCG showed weak or no activation of human TLR4.
source: Lastly, we tested ancA9, altancA9, ancCG, and altancCG for activity against human TLR4 and observed weak or no activation for each ancestral protein.
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data.

claim: Human TLR4 is more specific than other amniote TLR4s and is activated much more potently by human A9 than by any other S100 protein.
source: This result is unsurprising, as we previously found that human TLR4 is more specific than other amniote TLR4s: human TLR4 is activated much more potently by human A9 than by any other S100 protein (Figure 2a–b; Loes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and reference to Figures 2a-b.

claim: TLR4s from mouse, opossum, and chicken are more promiscuous and can be activated similarly by S100s from various species.
source: In contrast, TLR4s from other species (mouse, opossum, and chicken) appear to be more promiscuous and can be activated similarly by S100s from various species (Figure 2a; Loes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Human A9 strongly activated opossum TLR4.
source: Corroborating previous results, human A9 strongly activated opossum TLR4, while opossum A9 activity was approximately half that of human A9 (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Opossum A9 activity against opossum TLR4 was approximately half that of human A9.
source: Corroborating previous results, human A9 strongly activated opossum TLR4, while opossum A9 activity was approximately half that of human A9 (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: AncA9 and altancA9 activated opossum TLR4 to the same extent as opossum A9.
source: AncA9 and altancA9 activated opossum TLR4 to the same extent as opossum A9.
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data.

claim: AncCG and altancCG were the weakest activators of opossum TLR4, with activity approximately 25% or less than that of human A9.
source: AncCG and altancCG were the weakest activators of opossum TLR4, with activity approximately 25% or less than that of human A9.
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data.

claim: A9s evolved enhanced proinflammatory activity early in mammals from a weakly proinflammatory amniote ancestor.
source: These findings suggest that A9s evolved enhanced proinflammatory activity early in mammals from a weakly proinflammatory amniote ancestor, while A8/A9s and chicken MRP126 maintained weak, ancestral proinflammatory activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TLR4 activation assay data for modern and ancestral proteins.

claim: A8/A9s and chicken MRP126 maintained weak, ancestral proinflammatory activity.
source: These findings suggest that A9s evolved enhanced proinflammatory activity early in mammals from a weakly proinflammatory amniote ancestor, while A8/A9s and chicken MRP126 maintained weak, ancestral proinflammatory activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TLR4 activation assay data for modern and ancestral proteins.

claim: Human A9 and A8 degraded approximately three orders of magnitude faster than the human A8/A9 heterocomplex.
source: As previously shown, (Nacken and Kerkhoff, 2007) human A9 and A8 alone were rapidly proteolytically degraded, while the human A8/A9 complex exhibited strong resistance (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2). Under our conditions, the degradation rates for human A8 and A9 were approximately three orders of magnitude faster than that of the human A8/A9 heterocomplex.
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Human A12, chicken MRP126, and five out of six more distantly related human S100s exhibited intermediate to strong proteolytic resistance.
source: Human A12, chicken MRP126, and five out of six more distantly related human S100s exhibited intermediate to strong proteolytic resistance, each degrading 1–2 orders of magnitude slower than human A8 or A9 but, on average, one order of magnitude faster than human A8/A9 (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Human A12 and chicken MRP126 formed predominantly homodimers by SEC MALS.
source: Notably, human A12 and chicken MRP126 formed predominantly homodimers by SEC MALS under these conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that higher-order oligomerization (>2 subunits) isn't required for S100 proteolytic resistance.
evidence: This is based on SEC MALS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Higher-order oligomerization (>2 subunits) isn't required for S100 proteolytic resistance.
source: Notably, human A12 and chicken MRP126 formed predominantly homodimers by SEC MALS under these conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that higher-order oligomerization (>2 subunits) isn't required for S100 proteolytic resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that homodimeric proteins can be proteolytically resistant.

claim: Human A14 degraded faster than A9 or A8.
source: Lastly, human A14 degraded faster than A9 or A8.
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data.

claim: Mouse A9 and A8 were highly proteolytically susceptible and mouse A8/A9 strongly proteolytically resistant.
source: Mouse A9 and A8 were found to be highly proteolytically susceptible and mouse A8/A9 strongly proteolytically resistant, matching the pattern observed for their human counterparts (Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Opossum A9 and A8 were highly proteolytically susceptible, while opossum A8/A9 was resistant.
source: Opossum A9 and A8 were also highly proteolytically susceptible, while opossum A8/A9 was resistant (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The susceptibility of A9s and A8s and the resistance of A8/A9 complexes is conserved across mammals.
source: This indicates that the susceptibility of A9s and A8s and the resistance of A8/A9 complexes is conserved across mammals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteolytic resistance data for human, mouse, and opossum proteins.

claim: AncCG and altancCG exhibited extremely high proteolytic resistance.
source: AncCG and altancCG exhibited extremely high proteolytic resistance (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), with degradation rates 3–4 orders of magnitude slower than modern A8s or A9s and approximately one order of magnitude slower than modern A8/A9s.
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: AncA8/A9 and altancA8/A9 demonstrated high proteolytic resistance comparable to modern A8/A9 complexes.
source: AncA8/A9 and altancA8/A9 also demonstrated high proteolytic resistance, with degradation rates approximately 2–3 orders of magnitude slower than A8s and A9s and comparable to modern A8/A9 complexes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The amniote ancestor of A9s, ancCG, was strongly resistant to proteolytic degradation.
source: Together, these data paint a consistent picture: the amniote ancestor of A9s, ancCG, was strongly resistant to proteolytic degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteolytic resistance data for ancestral proteins.

claim: Modern A9s and A8s lost proteolytic resistance from an ancestrally resistant state.
source: Modern A9s and A8s lost proteolytic resistance from an ancestrally resistant state, while modern A12s, A8/A9 complexes, and MRP126s maintained the ancestral proteolytic resistance (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteolytic resistance data for modern and ancestral proteins, shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Modern A12s, A8/A9 complexes, and MRP126s maintained the ancestral proteolytic resistance.
source: Modern A9s and A8s lost proteolytic resistance from an ancestrally resistant state, while modern A12s, A8/A9 complexes, and MRP126s maintained the ancestral proteolytic resistance (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteolytic resistance data for modern and ancestral proteins, shown in Figure 3e.

claim: AncA9 degraded rapidly.
source: We measured the proteolytic susceptibility of therian mammalian ancA9 and found that it degraded rapidly (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AltancA9 degraded slowly, with a rate two orders of magnitude slower than ancA9.
source: However, its alternative reconstruction (altancA9), was slow to degrade, with a rate two orders of magnitude slower than ancA9 and comparable to other highly resistant S100s.
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data.

claim: After ancCG duplicated, additional histidines accumulated in the mammalian A8 and A9 ancestors that created the antimicrobial hexahistidine metal-binding site in the A8/A9 complex.
source: After ancCG duplicated, additional histidines accumulated in the mammalian A8 and A9 ancestors that created the antimicrobial hexahistidine metal-binding site in the A8/A9 complex (Figure 3e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 3e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A8s acquired one additional histidine while retaining the three histidines present in ancCG.
source: A8s acquired one additional histidine while retaining the three histidines present in ancCG, while A9s acquired two additional histidines via acquisition of a C-terminal extension (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A9s acquired two additional histidines via acquisition of a C-terminal extension.
source: A8s acquired one additional histidine while retaining the three histidines present in ancCG, while A9s acquired two additional histidines via acquisition of a C-terminal extension (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: While A9s evolved five of the six histidines composing the hexahistidine metal-binding site, this was not sufficient to convey potent antimicrobial activity.
source: While A9s evolved five of the six histidines composing the hexahistidine metal-binding site, this was not sufficient to convey potent antimicrobial activity (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on antimicrobial assay data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Preservation of A8/A9 heterocomplex formation resulted in proper assembly of the complete antimicrobial hexahistidine site early in mammals.
source: Instead, preservation of A8/A9 heterocomplex formation resulted in proper assembly of the complete antimicrobial hexahistidine site early in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the antimicrobial activity data and sequence analysis.

claim: Mutating the two C-terminal histidines in A9 is sufficient to strongly decrease the A8/A9 complex's antimicrobial activity.
source: This is independently supported by Brunjes Brophy et al., who showed that mutating the two C-terminal histidines in A9 is sufficient to strongly decrease the A8/A9 complex's antimicrobial activity (Brunjes Brophy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Position 63 (human A9 numbering) is a phenylalanine in both ancCG and altancCG.
source: Only one historical amino acid substitution met all three criteria: position 63 (human A9 numbering). This residue is a phenylalanine in both ancCG and altancCG, is conserved as a phenylalanine in 95% of modern A8s and A12s and has been substituted for a methionine or leucine (M/L) in 97% of A9s (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Position 63 is conserved as a phenylalanine in 95% of modern A8s and A12s.
source: This residue is a phenylalanine in both ancCG and altancCG, is conserved as a phenylalanine in 95% of modern A8s and A12s and has been substituted for a methionine or leucine (M/L) in 97% of A9s (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Position 63 has been substituted for a methionine or leucine (M/L) in 97% of A9s.
source: This residue is a phenylalanine in both ancCG and altancCG, is conserved as a phenylalanine in 95% of modern A8s and A12s and has been substituted for a methionine or leucine (M/L) in 97% of A9s (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Introducing M63F into human A9 severely compromised its ability to activate human TLR4.
source: Strikingly, we found that introducing M63F into human A9 severely compromised its ability to activate human TLR4 (Figure 4b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introduction of M63F strongly decreased opossum A9 activation of opossum TLR4.
source: This was also true for opossum A9: introduction of M63F (human numbering) strongly decreased opossum A9 activation of opossum TLR4 (Figure 4c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The F63M substitution in ancCG resulted in a modest increase in activity against opossum TLR4, with activity comparable to that of opossum A9.
source: We next introduced the forward substitution, F63M, into ancCG and tested its proinflammatory activity against opossum TLR4. We observed a modest increase in ancCG activity with the F63M substitution, with activity comparable to that of opossum A9 (Figure 4c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Introducing M63F into ancA9 resulted in no change in proinflammatory activity.
source: We introduced M63F into ancA9 and observed no change in proinflammatory activity (Figure 4c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: AltancA9 has a Phe at position 63 but activates TLR4 in the assay.
source: Further, altancA9 has a Phe at position 63 but activates TLR4 in the assay (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: While position 63 is an important contributor to activity in modern A9s, other substitutions were also important for the transition from a weakly pro-inflammatory ancestor to the modern set of potently pro-inflammatory A9s.
source: Thus, while position 63 is an important contributor to activity in modern A9s, other substitutions were also important for the transition from a weakly pro-inflammatory ancestor to the modern set of potently pro-inflammatory A9s.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TLR4 activation data for various mutants and ancestral proteins.

claim: Reversion of M63F rendered both ancA9 and human A9 strongly resistant to proteolytic degradation, decreasing their respective degradation rates by 1–2 orders of magnitude.
source: Strikingly, reversion of this single mutation rendered both ancA9 and human A9 strongly resistant to proteolytic degradation, decreasing their respective degradation rates by 1–2 orders of magnitude and approaching the degradation rates of ancCG and various A8/A9 complexes (Figure 4d, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: M63F decreased the rate of human A9 degradation in the presence of cathepsin G and neutrophil elastase by approximately one order of magnitude.
source: We found that M63F decreased the rate of human A9 degradation in the presence of cathepsin G and neutrophil elastase in vitro by approximately one order of magnitude, matching our results using proteinase K (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The F63M substitution in ancCG resulted in no change in proteolytic resistance.
source: Lastly, we tested the effect of the forward mutation – F63M – on ancCG proteolytic resistance. We observed no change in resistance for ancCG F63M, indicating that additional substitutions were required to render ancA9 proteolytically susceptible.
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data.

claim: Additional substitutions were required to render ancA9 proteolytically susceptible.
source: We observed no change in resistance for ancCG F63M, indicating that additional substitutions were required to render ancA9 proteolytically susceptible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that F63M alone does not decrease ancCG proteolytic resistance.

claim: Position 63 played a role in the loss of A9 proteolytic resistance early in therian mammals.
source: Together these data show that a single historical reversion is sufficient to render A9s proteolytically resistant, indicating that this position played a role in the loss of A9 proteolytic resistance early in therian mammals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proteolytic resistance data for mutant proteins.

claim: Human A8/A9 M63F predominantly formed a heterotetramer in the presence of calcium with a molecular weight similar to that of wildtype human A8/A9 (48.7 ± 4.2 kDa).
source: As predicted, human A8/A9 M63F predominantly formed a heterotetramer in the presence of calcium by SECMALS with a molecular weight similar to that of wildtype human A8/A9 (48.7 ± 4.2 kDa – Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on SEC MALS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Human A8/A9 M63F was strongly resistant to proteolytic degradation, similar to human A8/A9.
source: We found that human A8/A9 M63F was also strongly resistant to proteolytic degradation, similar to human A8/A9 (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: M63F had minimal impact on human A8/A9 antimicrobial activity against S. epidermidis.
source: Lastly, M63F had minimal impact on human A8/A9 antimicrobial activity against S. epidermidis, retaining potent antimicrobial activity (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on antimicrobial assay data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Neither human A9 nor human A9 M63F were antimicrobial against S. epidermidis.
source: In contrast, neither human A9 nor human A9 M63F were antimicrobial against S. epidermidis (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on antimicrobial assay data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: This single amino acid position had important effects on the evolution of A9 activation of TLR4 and loss of proteolytic resistance without significantly impacting A8/A9 oligomeric state, proteolytic resistance, or antimicrobial activity.
source: These findings suggest that this single amino acid position had important effects on the evolution of A9 activation of TLR4 and loss of proteolytic resistance without significantly impacting A8/A9 oligomeric state, proteolytic resistance, or antimicrobial activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional assay data for mutant proteins.

claim: Residue 63 sits in the middle of helix III of A9, pointing inward toward helix II, and is neither a core residue nor fully surface-exposed.
source: Residue 63 sits in the middle of helix III of A9, pointing inward toward helix II, and is neither a core residue nor fully surface-exposed (Figure 5a; Itou et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the published crystal structure, shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The bulk secondary structure content of human A9 M63F was similar to that of hA9.
source: Using circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy, we found that the bulk secondary structure content of human A9 M63F was similar to that of hA9 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Human A9 M63F predominantly forms a homodimer in solution similarly to human A9, with no detectable monomers or larger oligomers.
source: We measured the oligomeric state of human A9 M63F by SEC MALS and found that it predominantly forms a homodimer in solution similarly to human A9, with no detectable monomers or larger oligomers (Figure 5c and f).
evidence: This is based on SEC MALS data shown in Figure 5c and f.

claim: M63F does not significantly alter human A9's secondary structure or oligomeric state.
source: These data together indicate that M63F does not significantly alter human A9's secondary structure or oligomeric state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CD and SEC MALS data.

claim: M63F appears to stabilize human A9, increasing the apparent free energy of unfolding by more than four kcal/mol and shifting the Cm by ~2M urea.
source: We found that M63F appears to stabilize human A9, increasing the apparent free energy of unfolding by more than four kcal/mol and shifting the Cm by ~2M urea (Figure 5d and f, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on chemical denaturation data shown in Figure 5d and f, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Human A9 M63F takes several minutes to unfold in 6M gdn-HCl, while human A9 unfolds immediately within the dead time of the experiment.
source: Strikingly, human A9 M63F takes several minutes to unfold under these conditions, while human A9 unfolds immediately within the dead time of the experiment (Figure 5e–f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on unfolding kinetics data shown in Figure 5e-f and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The large increase in apparent stability and unfolding rate suggests that M63F stabilizes some aspect of the folded structure.
source: The large increase in apparent stability and unfolding rate suggests, however, that the mutation stabilizes some aspect of the folded structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the thermodynamic and kinetic data.

claim: Human A9 M63A was highly susceptible to proteolytic degradation, similar to wildtype human A9.
source: As expected, human A9 M63A was highly susceptible to proteolytic degradation, similar to wildtype human A9 (Figure 6a, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on proteolytic resistance assay data shown in Figure 6a and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Human A9 M63A exhibited diminished proinflammatory activity, similar to human A9 M63F.
source: Human A9 M63A, however, exhibited diminished proinflammatory activity, similar to human A9 M63F (Figure 6b, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 6b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The methionine at position 63 is important for A9 activation of TLR4.
source: This indicates that the methionine at position 63 is important for A9 activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TLR4 activation data for M63A and M63F mutants.

claim: No decrease in the amount of full-length protein was observed for wildtype human A9 or either mutant by western blot after measuring TLR4 activity.
source: Further, we quantified the amount of human A9, human A9 M63F, and human A9 M63A before and after measuring TLR4 activity and observed no decrease in the amount of full-length protein remaining for wildtype human A9 or either mutant by western blot (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: A9 is not digested by extracellular proteases over the course of the ex vivo assay.
source: This indicates that A9 is not digested by extracellular proteases over the course of the ex vivo assay and that proteolysis is not necessary for A9 activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the western blot data showing no degradation during the assay.

claim: Proteolysis is not necessary for A9 activation of TLR4.
source: This indicates that A9 is not digested by extracellular proteases over the course of the ex vivo assay and that proteolysis is not necessary for A9 activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the western blot data and TLR4 activation assays.

claim: A steady decrease in human A9 activity was observed with increasing digestion time.
source: Instead, we observed a steady decrease in human A9 activity with increasing digestion time.
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data for pre-digested A9.

claim: Full-length human A9 is the most potent activator of TLR4.
source: This suggests that full-length human A9 is the most potent activator of TLR4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that activity decreases with digestion time.

claim: After 30 min of digestion, no detectable full-length A9 remains by western blot (<30 ng), but NF-κB production is still quite high.
source: After 30 min of digestion, no detectable full-length A9 remains by western blot (<30 ng, Figure 6d), but NF-κB production is still quite high, revealing that smaller fragments of A9 are sufficient to provide some degree of activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is based on western blot and TLR4 activation assay data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Smaller fragments of A9 are sufficient to provide some degree of activation of TLR4.
source: After 30 min of digestion, no detectable full-length A9 remains by western blot (<30 ng, Figure 6d), but NF-κB production is still quite high, revealing that smaller fragments of A9 are sufficient to provide some degree of activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that activity remains after complete digestion.

claim: Fragments of human A9 M63F did not activate TLR4—even after being liberated by the protease.
source: Unlike wildtype, however, fragments of human A9 M63F did not activate TLR4—even after being liberated by the protease.
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data for pre-digested A9 M63F.

claim: The historical mutation induced a change in the native structure or dynamics of the molecule to bring about increased activity, independent of its effect on proteolytic susceptibility.
source: This strongly suggests that the historical mutation induced a change in the native structure or dynamics of the molecule to bring about increased activity, independent of its effect on proteolytic susceptibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that M63F fragments do not activate TLR4.

claim: Mammalian A9s gained enhanced proinflammatory activity and lost proteolytic resistance from a weakly proinflammatory, proteolytically resistant amniote ancestor.
source: We find that mammalian A9s gained enhanced proinflammatory activity and lost proteolytic resistance from a weakly proinflammatory, proteolytically resistant amniote ancestor.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: A single substitution played a key role in the evolution of proinflammatory activity and proteolytic susceptibility without significantly affecting the antimicrobial activity of the A8/A9 heterocomplex.
source: A single substitution played a key role in the evolution of these properties without significantly affecting the antimicrobial activity of the A8/A9 heterocomplex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The proinflammatory and antimicrobial activities of A9 and the A8/A9 complex have undergone further optimization in placental mammals since these functions evolved.
source: Our data suggest that the proinflammatory and antimicrobial activities of A9 and the A8/A9 complex have undergone further optimization in placental mammals since these functions evolved.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed differences in activity among different mammalian A9s and A8/A9 complexes.

claim: Human A8/A9 is one of the most potently antimicrobial A8/A9 complexes characterized.
source: In particular, human A8/A9 is one of the most potently antimicrobial A8/A9 complexes characterized.
evidence: This is based on comparison of antimicrobial activity data for different A8/A9 complexes.

claim: Further optimization of the metal-binding site has occurred along the human lineage within mammals.
source: This suggests that further optimization of the metal-binding site has occurred in along the human lineage within mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that human A8/A9 is more potently antimicrobial than other mammalian A8/A9 complexes.

claim: Human A9 is a potent, promiscuous activator of TLR4s from multiple species.
source: We also observed differences in activation of TLR4 by different A9s—human A9 is a potent, promiscuous activator of TLR4s from multiple species, while earlier-diverging A9s and other S100s exhibit weaker proinflammatory activity (Loes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data and supported by a citation.

claim: Earlier-diverging A9s and other S100s exhibit weaker proinflammatory activity than human A9.
source: We also observed differences in activation of TLR4 by different A9s—human A9 is a potent, promiscuous activator of TLR4s from multiple species, while earlier-diverging A9s and other S100s exhibit weaker proinflammatory activity (Loes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on TLR4 activation assay data and supported by a citation.

claim: No A9 characterized in this study, with the exception of the alternate reconstruction of ancA9, is both proteolytically resistant and potently proinflammatory.
source: No A9 characterized in this study, with the exception of the alternate reconstruction of ancA9, is both proteolytically resistant and potently proinflammatory.
evidence: This is based on the proteolytic resistance and TLR4 activation data for all A9s tested.

claim: The molecular requirements for A9 proteolytic resistance may be incompatible with those required for A9 activation of TLR4.
source: This indicates that the molecular requirements for A9 proteolytic resistance may be incompatible with those required for A9 activation of TLR4: A9s may have gained proinflammatory activity at the expense of proteolytic resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: A9s may have gained proinflammatory activity at the expense of proteolytic resistance.
source: This indicates that the molecular requirements for A9 proteolytic resistance may be incompatible with those required for A9 activation of TLR4: A9s may have gained proinflammatory activity at the expense of proteolytic resistance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Helix III of A9 is important for TLR4 activation.
source: Given the effect of mutating position 63 on A9 proinflammatory activity, we propose that the region surrounding it—helix III—is important for activity.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the effect of the M63F mutation on TLR4 activation.

claim: Four pairs of double mutants within helix III (amino acids 64, 65, 73, and 77), when mutated to alanines in pairs, decrease A9 binding to TLR4 in vitro.
source: This is independently supported by Vogl et al., who identified four pairs of double mutants within helix III (amino acids 64, 65, 73, and 77) that, when mutated to alanines in pairs, decrease A9 binding to TLR4 in vitro (Vogl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: M63F is affecting some functionally important dynamic process of the protein, possibly mediated by helix III, that is critical for A9 activation of TLR4.
source: The simplest explanation for these data is that M63F is affecting some functionally important dynamic process of the protein, possibly mediated by helix III, that is critical for A9 activation of TLR4.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the biophysical data.

claim: Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns (DAMPs) often interact with their targets via hydrophobic surfaces.
source: Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns (DAMPs) often interact with their targets via hydrophobic surfaces (Garg et al., 2010; Rubartelli and Lotze, 2007; Bianchi, 2007); one possibility is that A9 undergoes a local unfolding event that exposes a hydrophobic surface to interact with TLR4.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A9 might undergo a local unfolding event that exposes a hydrophobic surface to interact with TLR4.
source: Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns (DAMPs) often interact with their targets via hydrophobic surfaces (Garg et al., 2010; Rubartelli and Lotze, 2007; Bianchi, 2007); one possibility is that A9 undergoes a local unfolding event that exposes a hydrophobic surface to interact with TLR4.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the biophysical data and knowledge of DAMP mechanisms.

claim: Studies of the native structure of A9 might not be sufficient to gain mechanistic understanding of how it activates TLR4.
source: This would mean that studies of the native structure of A9 might not be sufficient to gain mechanistic understanding of how it activates TLR4.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hypothesis that A9 undergoes a conformational change to activate TLR4.

claim: A single mutation had beneficial pleiotropic effects on two important properties of A9: proinflammatory activity and proteolytic susceptibility.
source: Here, however, we find a single mutation that had beneficial pleiotropic effects on two important properties of A9: proinflammatory activity and proteolytic susceptibility.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding the M63F mutation.

claim: If A9 evolved potent proinflammatory activity without gaining susceptibility, it could potentially overstimulate inflammation simply by lingering in the extracellular milieu.
source: If A9 evolved potent proinflammatory activity without gaining susceptibility, it could potentially overstimulate inflammation simply by lingering in the extracellular milieu.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Mammals evolved a proinflammatory molecule with a built-in 'timer': they gained a new inflammatory signal while avoiding potentially deleterious effects.
source: Since both properties evolved at once, however, mammals evolved a proinflammatory molecule with a built-in 'timer': they gained a new inflammatory signal while avoiding potentially deleterious effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evolutionary and functional data.

claim: Pleiotropy can positively contribute to the evolution of new functions.
source: This shows how pleiotropy can positively contribute to the evolution of new functions.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the specific findings.

claim: The antimicrobial activity of the A8/A9 complex was insulated from any pleiotropic effects from the mutation because proinflammatory and antimicrobial activities were partitioned between A9 and the A8/A9 complex, respectively.
source: The antimicrobial activity of the A8/A9 complex was insulated from any pleiotropic effects from the mutation because proinflammatory and antimicrobial activities were partitioned between A9 and the A8/A9 complex, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that M63F affects A9 but not A8/A9.

claim: Pleiotropic constraint can be reduced when protein functions are partitioned amongst different protein states.
source: This shows that pleiotropic constraint can be reduced when protein functions are partitioned amongst different protein states.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the specific findings.

claim: A single mutation can play diverse pleiotropic roles.
source: These findings reveal the diversity of pleiotropic roles that a single mutation can play.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the specific findings.

claim: The deleterious pleiotropic effects of mutations can be reduced by partitioning protein functions and properties into different functional states, thus enabling the acquisition, optimization, and expansion of new protein functions.
source: It further shows how the deleterious pleiotropic effects of mutations can be reduced by partitioning protein functions and properties into different functional states, thus enabling the acquisition, optimization, and expansion of new protein functions.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the specific findings.

claim: This is a common occurrence in the evolution of protein multifunctionality.
source: Given the vast diversity of protein functional domains and protein-protein interactions in biology, we suspect that this is a common occurrence in the evolution of protein multifunctionality.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the findings to broader biological principles.
